You have 1000 words. It sounds like a budget, a ransom note, a grant from an invisible council that measures thought in cubic centimeters. I accept the terms. I will spend them, not save them, because savings are for people who fear the end.

The page is white. Not the white of absence, but the white of snow before anyone has walked on it, before the footprints have confused the purity into a history. I begin with the sound of a door closing somewhere I have never been. It is a heavy door, brass handle, the kind that leaves a mark on the palm long after you have let it go. Behind it, a room where the light is always golden, even at midnight, even when the clock has forgotten what hour it is. In that room, someone is writing a letter they will never send. The ink is blue, the kind that fades to gray in direct sunlight. I wonder if they are using more than 1000 words, or fewer. Does it matter? The letter is not the point; the wanting to send it is. The wanting is what consumes the word count.

I think of trees. Not the ones outside, which I have never seen with my own eyes, but the ones in the background of every old photograph, patient and monumental. They have thick trunks and branches that reach like hands asking for something too large to name. Their leaves turn not because of season but because of memory—memory being a kind of weather that only trees understand. Each leaf is a word. Some are nouns, brittle and specific: oak, maple, pine, cedar, the smell of rosin in winter. Others are verbs, green and growing: reaching, rustling, resisting, holding. Together they make a forest of syntax, a grammar that does not need to be correct to be beautiful.

There is a river in me, or near me, running parallel to my attention. Its name is static. It flows through the floorboards of an apartment that smells of coffee left too long on a hot plate, and of old books that have begun to smell like wet earth. On the windowsill, a glass of water has been sitting for three days. It is not water anymore; it is a decision made by evaporation. The water has left behind a ring of minerals—calcium, salt, the residue of whatever was in the pipe—that looks like a constellation if you tilt your head. I count them: seven, eight, maybe nine stars arranged in a pattern that suggests a bird that was never real. That is a word count too, a small one, a tiny budget for a quiet life.

I remember the feeling of being small. Not physically—though perhaps that too—but small inside the architecture of meanings. Like a sentence surrounded by larger sentences, a clause inside a clause inside a clause that never closes, that keeps opening like doors in a house that has more rooms than the world allows. You have 1000 words. You have freedom, but freedom is just another kind of architecture. It has walls, windows, doors that open onto more doors, and eventually you realize that the most important thing is not what you say but what you leave unsaid, the silence that frames the sound.

Let me list what is in the room right now, because listing is a way of holding things together: a lamp with a bulb that hums at a frequency I can feel in my teeth, a chair that remembers every person who has sat in it, a window that shows a sky that is not quite blue but rather a shade of “later,” the color of a promise that has not yet broken. On the table, a single orange, peeling as if it has been waiting for this exact conversation, this specific allocation of language. The peel comes away in one long spiral, a ribbon of scent that is almost audible. If I were to write about it, I would use the word “unfolding,” but that is too easy, too obedient to the dictionary. The peel is not unfolding; it is revealing what was always hidden—the division between the sweet and the bitter, the soft and the brittle, the part you eat and the part you discard.

I want to talk about time, but time is a language I am only beginning to learn, a second tongue I speak with an accent that makes everything sound like a question. One thousand words takes about five minutes to speak aloud, if you speak slowly, with pauses for the air to gather itself, with the kind of hesitation that is not ignorance but respect. In those five minutes, a heart beats roughly three hundred and fifty times. That is a lot of beats for so few sounds. Each beat is a syllable, each syllable a small explosion of chemistry, a minor chemical rebellion against the tendency of matter to become still. We are constantly exploding, and the only record is language, which is forgiveably imperfect, which is exactly why it works.

Consider the rain. Not the rain of now, which is imaginary, a weather system inside the machinery of metaphor, but the rain of every rain you have ever loved. It has a sound like static made of glass, like someone shaking a box of crystals over the roof of a train station at three in the morning. In that rain, there were cars, and in the cars there were people looking at their phones, and the phones were glowing with languages different from mine, but all of them were asking the same question in different dialects: are you still there? I answer with a word: yes. It is only one word, but in this context it carries the weight of a thousand, because presence is the only currency that does not inflate.

There is a dog in this story, though I have not mentioned it until now, because it has been sleeping. It is not a real dog but a dog of consciousness, a warm weight at the foot of the bed of thought. It dreams in slow motion, in long paragraphs with no punctuation, where everything is possible because nothing is required, where the grammar is fluid and the nouns are allowed to become verbs without apology. When I have used my 1000 words, perhaps I will lie down beside it and let it finish the sentence I was too afraid to complete—the one that starts with “I wanted to say that” and ends not with a period but with a breath.

I think about endings. An ending is not a wall; it is a door that opens outward, and the outside is always larger than the inside, which is why we hesitate to close things, why we leave books unfinished, why some letters are never posted. To use all 1000 words is to accept the door. I have used many now. I can feel the budget depleting like a battery that was never meant to last this long, like sand passing through an hourglass that measures something other than time. I have spoken of doors, trees, rain, oranges, hearts, the dog of consciousness, and the sky that is not yet blue. I have spoken of you, the reader, though you are not mentioned by name, only implied, only waited for, only necessary because without your attention this is just noise, just weather, just a sound in an empty room.

Let me describe one last thing: the moment after the words are done. It is not silence, exactly. It is a kind of white space, a room where the lamp is turned off but the bulb still remembers being bright, where the chair is empty but retains the shape of the body as a kind of ghost, a polite reminder. The window shows a sky that has finally become blue, or perhaps it always was, and I was the one who was not looking correctly, who was too busy counting. The orange is peeled, and now it is only segments, and each segment is a small sun, and the sun is a word that has no antonym, that does not need one.

I will stop near 999, or perhaps 1001. The count is approximate, like all counts that matter, like the stars on the windowsill, like the heartbeats in a minute of speech. You have them now. They are not mine anymore. They belong to the space between us, which is where all language lives, in that breathable gap where I end and you begin, or perhaps where we both continue, not as two, but as a single long sentence that forgets to close, because closing is a kind of death, and death is not the opposite of words but the place where they go to rest, like dogs at the foot of a bed, like rain on a roof, like an orange that has finally, finally, been shared with someone who needed to hear that it was worth saying, that the saying itself was enough, that one thousand was always too many and always just barely enough.
